passage: Lokesh ran a mobile repair shop in a small town and thought he knew phones. One day his sister Jaya got a message: "Your electricity will be cut tonight. Call this number." Lokesh laughed at first, then paused. Their neighbour had lost money to a message like this. Jaya almost called. Lokesh took the phone and checked the number; it wasn't the electricity board. "It's a trick," he said. "They want you to panic." That evening he helped her set a strong password on her email, turn on two-step login, and check which apps could see her contacts. Jaya was surprised how many had access. "I never agreed to this," she said. "You did," he said, "when you clicked 'allow' without reading."

qa.q: What did the message to Jaya say?
qa.a: It said her electricity would be cut tonight and to call a number.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh pause after laughing?
qa.a: He remembered their neighbour losing money to a similar message, which made him take it seriously.

qa.q: What steps did Lokesh take to protect Jaya's accounts?
qa.a: He set a strong password, turned on two-step login, and checked which apps could access her contacts.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel about her phone's permissions now?
qa.a: She was surprised and perhaps uneasy to learn she had allowed access without reading, and may be more careful next time.

grounding: It shows young adults recognising a phishing message and protecting accounts and data permissions.

passage: Ivan was a student in Warsaw and had just signed up for a new music app. It asked for access to his contacts, location, microphone and photos. He clicked "yes" to everything, as usual. His friend Priscila, studying law, looked over his shoulder. "Why does a music app need your photos?" Ivan shrugged. "Everyone does it." She showed him the privacy settings. "You can say no. And you can ask what data they keep." Ivan was annoyed but curious. He went through his phone and found a torch app that could see his location. He turned it off. A week later, he got a fake email pretending to be his bank. Because Priscila had made him paranoid, he checked the sender first. It was fake.

qa.q: What did the music app ask access to?
qa.a: It asked for access to his contacts, location, microphone and photos.

qa.q: Why was Ivan annoyed but curious?
qa.a: He didn't like being questioned about his habits, but Priscila's point made him wonder what he had actually agreed to.

qa.q: What habits helped Ivan protect himself?
qa.a: Checking app permissions, refusing ones that aren't needed, and checking the sender of emails helped him avoid the bank scam.

qa.q: How might Priscila feel when Ivan tells her about the fake email?
qa.a: She'd probably feel pleased and a bit amused that her "paranoia" rubbed off on him.

grounding: It shows a young man learning about data consent and recognising phishing.

passage: At the call centre in Noida, Asif was new and eager. On his third day, a message popped up on his work chat: "IT team here. We need your login password to update your system." Asif was about to type it in. Vijay, a senior colleague at the next desk, glanced over. "Stop. IT never asks for passwords." Asif's face went red. "But it says IT." "Anyone can type that," Vijay said. He showed Asif how to report it to the real IT desk. Later, the manager sent an email to everyone: a phishing attempt had targeted new staff. Asif felt shaken but grateful. That evening he changed his personal passwords too, which he'd been using for years.

qa.q: On which day did the message pop up for Asif?
qa.a: It popped up on his third day.

qa.q: Why did Asif's face go red?
qa.a: He was embarrassed that he had nearly given away his password to a fake message.

qa.q: What did Vijay do that helped Asif?
qa.a: He stopped him, explained that IT never asks for passwords, and showed him how to report it properly.

qa.q: How might Asif's manager see the incident?
qa.a: The manager might be relieved it was reported quickly, and see it as a reason to train new staff about phishing.

grounding: It shows a young man learning to recognise phishing at work and protect his accounts.

passage:
Hi Aditi,
Writing this so you don't fall for what nearly got me. Yesterday I got an email 'from the university' saying my scholarship would be cancelled unless I verified my login within two hours. The logo looked right. I was already typing my password when I noticed the sender address ended in something odd, not our college domain. My heart was thumping. I closed it and called the scholarship office instead; they said they never ask for passwords by email. Then I changed my password, turned on the two-step code, and stopped using one password for everything (yes, I know, you told me). Also, that free quiz app you sent last week wanted my contacts and location. I said no. Stay suspicious, okay?
Love,
Zainab

qa.q: What did the fake email say would happen to Zainab's scholarship?
qa.a: It said Zainab's scholarship would be cancelled unless the login was verified within two hours.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling on noticing the odd sender address?
qa.a: Alarmed, with a thumping heart, on realising the password was about to go to a stranger.

qa.q: Which of Zainab's steps would protect Aditi too?
qa.a: Checking the sender, contacting the office through a known route, using different passwords with a two-step code, and refusing app permissions that are not needed.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel reading this email?
qa.a: Maybe a little pleased to have been right about passwords, but also shaken and grateful for the warning 🙂

grounding: An email shows a student recognising a phishing message, securing the account and refusing unneeded data permissions.

passage: Dilnaz, remember how you laughed at me at the fest registration desk? 'Zeenat and her paper forms!' Let me explain. The form had this tiny line at the bottom, already ticked: 'I agree to share my details with our partners.' Partners who? The boy at the desk didn't know. So I unticked it and asked for a paper form. You all went ahead on the tablet. Two weeks later you were getting calls about loans and coaching classes, remember? My phone stayed quiet. I'm not a genius. I learnt the hard way last year, when a free photo-editing app asked for my gallery, contacts and location and I clicked yes to everything. Now I read what I'm agreeing to, at least the tick-boxes. If they can't tell me why they need it, they don't get it.

qa.q: What did the pre-ticked line on the registration form say?
qa.a: 'I agree to share my details with our partners.'

qa.q: Why did Zeenat insist on a paper form even though she was laughed at?
qa.a: She was wary after giving an app everything last year, and she did not want her details going to partners no one could name.

qa.q: What rule does Zeenat now follow, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: If they cannot explain why they need her data, she does not give it; reading the tick-boxes lets her control who gets her information.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see the incident now?
qa.a: After the calls about loans and coaching, she probably sees Zeenat's caution as sensible rather than fussy.

grounding: A young woman explains to a friend how she learned to read and refuse data-sharing consent.

passage: I'm Lavanya, Ayesha's roommate. Last Tuesday I watched her nearly click a link, and then not. A text had come: "Your bank KYC expires today. Update now or account will be blocked," with a link. Ayesha's scholarship money was in that account; I know because she'd waited weeks for it. Her thumb hovered over the link. Then she put the phone face down on the bed and sat very still. After a minute she opened the bank's own app, not the link, and found no notice. She called the number printed on her debit card. They told her it was a scam. She reported the text on the government's cyber-crime portal and changed her password anyway. She didn't say much. She just made two cups of tea and handed me one. I'd never seen her hands that unsteady over a teacup.

qa.q: What did the text say would happen if Ayesha didn't update?
qa.a: The account would be blocked.

qa.q: What might Ayesha have been feeling while her thumb hovered over the link?
qa.a: Ayesha was probably frightened for the scholarship money and torn between panic and suspicion, which is why she stopped and sat still.

qa.q: Which of Ayesha's steps could others copy?
qa.a: Not clicking, checking the bank's own app, calling the number on the card, reporting the text and changing the password.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see the moment from the outside?
qa.a: Lavanya notices the unsteady hands and the silence and can only guess at the fear, but clearly admires how carefully Ayesha acted.

grounding: A roommate watches a student recognise a phishing text, verify through official channels and report it.

passage:
Monday. Anjali used the same password for everything: her college portal, her email, the food app. Ujjwal teased her about it in the canteen. "Nobody wants my account," she laughed.
Thursday. A message went out from her own email to all her contacts, asking for money for a "medical emergency". Her Mausi called in a panic. Anjali's stomach dropped. With Ujjwal beside her in the college lab, she reset the email password, turned on two-step login, and posted a warning to everyone.
The following Sunday. She sat with a notebook and went through her accounts one by one: a different long passphrase for each, stored in a password manager. Then she opened her phone settings and saw that a torch app had access to her contacts and location. She switched it off. "Why did I ever say yes to that?" she muttered. Ujjwal didn't tease this time.

qa.q: What did the message from Anjali's email ask for?
qa.a: Money for a medical emergency.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when Mausi called in a panic?
qa.a: Anjali felt her stomach drop, shocked and frightened that her account had been used to trick her family.

qa.q: What did Anjali change that protects her from now on?
qa.a: A different long passphrase for each account in a password manager, two-step login, and removing permissions apps don't need.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see Anjali by the Sunday?
qa.a: Ujjwal sees she has taken it seriously and is doing the hard work, so teasing no longer feels right; he likely feels sympathetic.

grounding: Over a week, a student goes from reusing one password to securing her accounts and reviewing app permissions after a hack.

passage: Zainab, you young people think only old uncles fall for these calls. Listen. When I was branch manager in Kochi, a college boy, Anand, came in shaking. Someone had called "from the bank" saying his account would be frozen, and asked for the OTP to "verify". Anand was sharp, top of his engineering class. He gave it. Why? Because the caller knew his name, his birthday, even his last transaction. People forget how much they have scattered about themselves online. We blocked the card in time, luckily. But Anand's real lesson came after. He went home and removed his birthday, phone number and hometown from every public profile. He told me, "I handed them the key years ago, bit by bit." So, Zainab, before you fill in that online quiz asking your first pet's name, think of Anand. Your Karthik Uncle has seen what happens next.

qa.q: What did the caller ask Anand for?
qa.a: The OTP, to verify.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he came into the branch?
qa.a: Anand was shaking, frightened and probably ashamed that a clever student like him had been tricked.

qa.q: What was Anand's turning point after the call, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Removing his birthday, number and hometown from public profiles, because scammers build trust from such scattered details.

qa.q: How might Karthik, as branch manager, have felt seeing Anand shaking?
qa.a: Karthik likely felt concerned and protective, acting quickly to block the card, and wanted Anand to see it wasn't about intelligence.

grounding: A retired bank manager tells a young woman how a student fell for an OTP scam and then cut back his public data.

passage:
It was 11:55 p.m. An email arrived for Mohit: "Your bank account will be blocked at midnight. Update KYC now." There was a link and the bank's logo.
Mohit panicked. Midnight was five minutes away. He clicked. The page asked for his card number and OTP.
He paused. His cousin Manjula, who worked in a bank, had told him: "Banks never ask for OTP."
He looked closely. The sender's address was a long string of random letters.
He closed the page, called the bank's official number from the back of his card, and they confirmed it was phishing. He forwarded it to the bank's report address and changed his password.
He texted Manjula: "Almost fell for it." She replied, "You didn't. That's what matters."

qa.q: What did the page ask for?
qa.a: His card number and OTP.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he clicked the link?
qa.a: Mohit felt panicked by the midnight deadline.

qa.q: What steps did Mohit take after noticing the warning signs?
qa.a: He closed the page, called the official bank number, reported the email and changed his password.

qa.q: How does Manjula see Mohit's near miss?
qa.a: Manjula focuses on the fact that he stopped in time, not on the mistake of clicking.

grounding: Under time pressure a young man spots a phishing email and reports it.

passage:
Amandeep got a message from her friend Dolma: "Why did you send me a weird link?"
Amandeep hadn't. Someone had got into her social account.
She realised she'd used the same password for everything since school: her birthday and her dog's name.
Dolma came over to her Chandigarh flat. "Change all your passwords. Different ones. Use a password manager. And turn on two-step login."
Amandeep spent the evening doing it. It took hours. She also checked which apps had access to her account and removed six she didn't recognise.
"I feel exposed," she said.
"You fixed it fast," said Dolma. "That's the important part."

qa.q: How many apps did Amandeep remove access for?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when she said she felt exposed?
qa.a: Amandeep felt vulnerable and uneasy after being hacked.

qa.q: What steps did Dolma suggest to protect Amandeep's accounts?
qa.a: Using different passwords, a password manager, two-step login, and removing unknown app access.

qa.q: How does Dolma see Amandeep's response?
qa.a: Dolma thinks acting quickly is what matters most.

grounding: A young woman learns password safety after her account is hacked.

passage:
"Himani, this new photo-editing app wants access to your contacts, location and microphone."
"So? It's free."
"Why does a photo app need your microphone?" asked Jaya.
Himani frowned. "I didn't read that."
"Free apps often make money from your data. Read the permissions."
"Nobody reads those."
"That's why they get away with it."
Himani scrolled. Buried in the terms: "We may share data with partners."
"Ugh," she said. She denied contacts, location and mic access. The app still worked.
"See? It didn't even need them."
Himani went through her other apps that night. She switched off access for eight of them.

qa.q: Which three kinds of access did the app want?
qa.a: Contacts, location and microphone.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she said "Ugh"?
qa.a: Himani felt annoyed and uneasy about her data being shared.

qa.q: What habit did Jaya encourage?
qa.a: Reading app permissions and denying access that the app doesn't need.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel when Himani checks all her apps?
qa.a: Jaya probably feels glad her friend took data consent seriously.

grounding: A young woman learns to review app permissions and understand data consent.

passage:
In my second year, an email arrived that looked exactly like our university portal: logo, colours, even the registrar's signature. "Your scholarship will be cancelled unless you verify your account in 24 hours." There was a login button.
My hands went cold. I needed that scholarship.
Then I hovered over the button. The link went to a strange address with extra letters. Our portal never asked for passwords by email.
I didn't click. I called the scholarship office, and they said it was fake and had already hit two hundred students. My brother Vikas, who works in IT, came over that weekend and made me change my reused password everywhere, set up two-step login, and use a password manager.
I'm Parul, and now I hover over every link before I click. Even the real ones.

qa.q: What did the email say would happen in 24 hours?
qa.a: The scholarship would be cancelled unless the account was verified.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when the email arrived?
qa.a: Parul felt a cold rush of fear, needing that scholarship badly.

qa.q: Which steps protected Parul, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Hovering to check the link, calling the office directly, then changing reused passwords and adding two-step login, because they stop both this attack and future ones.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt hearing about the email?
qa.a: Vikas was probably alarmed but relieved Parul didn't click, and keen to make the accounts safer.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult recognising a phishing email and strengthening account security.

passage:
IT help desk note. Deepika, systems officer, college campus.
Mridul, final-year student, came in panicking: his college email had been used to send spam to the whole department, and his cloud drive password was changed. He said he'd used the same password "for everything since Class 10".
We locked the account, reset it with a new strong password, and turned on two-step login. I showed him how one leaked site can open every account when passwords are reused.
He was very embarrassed. "I thought I was too boring to hack."
I told him it's automatic; attackers try leaked passwords everywhere. We listed his important accounts together, and he changed them in front of me, one by one. He also asked about an app that wanted his contacts; I suggested reading what it asks for before agreeing.
He'll send a short note to the department apologising for the spam.

qa.q: How long had Mridul used the same password?
qa.a: "For everything since Class 10".

qa.q: What does Mridul's "I thought I was too boring to hack" reveal about how he felt?
qa.a: It reveals Mridul felt embarrassed and caught off guard, having believed he wasn't a target.

qa.q: What practical lessons from Deepika could help other students?
qa.a: Use a different strong password for each account, turn on two-step login, and read what an app asks for before agreeing.

qa.q: How might the department see Mridul's apology note?
qa.a: Most would probably understand and appreciate that he explained and fixed the problem.

grounding: Shows an IT officer helping a young adult recover a hacked account and learn about password reuse and data consent.

passage:
Sunday
Yash writing. Downloaded a new fitness app today. Before it would even show me a workout, it wanted: my contacts, my location "always", my microphone, and my photos.
Why does a push-up app need my microphone??
Sachin laughed at me. "Just press allow, bro, everyone does."
But I remembered the workshop at college: every "allow" is you giving data away, and some apps sell it. So I read the privacy page. It said they "may share data with partners for advertising". Very vague.
I said no to contacts, microphone and photos, and chose "only while using" for location. The app still worked fine.
Sachin tried the same thing on his phone. Now he's annoyed at how many apps have his contacts. We spent an hour going through settings. Weirdly fun.

qa.q: Which permissions did Yash refuse?
qa.a: Contacts, microphone and photos.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the app asked for the microphone?
qa.a: Yash felt suspicious and puzzled, wondering why a push-up app needed it.

qa.q: What did Yash's approach show about data consent?
qa.a: Reading what an app asks for and allowing only what it really needs gives informed consent, instead of pressing allow by habit.

qa.q: How does Sachin feel after checking his own phone?
qa.a: Sachin feels annoyed and a bit alarmed at how many apps already have his contacts.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult understanding app permissions as data consent and limiting what gets shared.
